On what would have been his 48th birthday, the sports world honored late Los Angeles Lakers legend Kobe Bryant on Sunday.

Several sports-related accounts and fans took to X on Sunday to celebrate the life and legacy of Bryant through a series of posts:

Bryant died in January 2020 at the age of 41 in a helicopter crash that also took the life of his 13-year-old daughter Gianna.

Nicknamed The Black Mamba, Kobe established himself as one of the greatest players in NBA history during his 20-year run with the Lakers.

Bryant was an 18-time All-Star, 15-time All-NBA selection, five-time NBA champion, four-time All-Star Game MVP, two-time scoring champion, two-time NBA Finals MVP and one-time NBA MVP.

He is also fourth on the NBA's all-time scoring list with 33,643 points, placing him behind only LeBron James, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Karl Malone.

Kobe even transcended the world of sports in 2018 when he won an Oscar for best animated short film with Dear Basketball .

articles.title: Everything Caitlin Clark, Stephanie White Said After Fever's Loss to Breanna Stewart, Liberty
articles.summary: Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White wants to see more consistency from her squad following a 109-102 loss to the New York Liberty on Saturday.
articles.body:
Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White wants to see more consistency from her squad following a 109-102 loss to the New York Liberty on Saturday.

"I thought that there were some moments where we made them uncomfortable. Not enough," White told reporters in her post-game press conference. "When we were up into the ball pressuring, I thought we got some really good things on the defensive end. And then there were lapses, lapses that caused fouls that went to free throws. Lapses that allowed offensive rebounds. Lapses that allowed soft switches into cuts. Lapses on the offensive end where we didn't move the ball. We didn't find the right play, didn't find the right pass."

No Cunningham-Carrington Issues in Rematch (AP)

White cited how the Fever shot 57.1 percent overall and went 11-of-26 on three-pointers, yet came out on the losing end.

"More than anything, I think this is just an opportunity for us to keep learning how much of a sense of urgency you have to play with every single possession," she said. "This is playoff basketball right now and there has to be an urgency every single possession."

The Fever are in the fourth leg of a five-game road trip, which got underway on Aug. 16. Star Caitlin Clark didn't want to use the schedule as an excuse for the team's showing against New York.

"Yeah our schedule's tough — I think we play more back-to-backs than just about anybody in the league," she said. "But it is what it is. … Everybody's tired. Everybody's sore. Who cares? Figure out a way to make yourself feel better and suit up and go play."

Clark finished with 21 points, four rebounds and seven assists. She was one of three Fever players to score 20-plus points, joining Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston. Mitchell added to her WNBA record by doing it for the 22nd straight game.

"I think it says what a high level that she's playing at," White said of the dynamic guard. "I think it shows how difficult it is to guard her one-on-one. I think the biggest thing for me is how she's doing it in a lot of different ways. You used to play Kelsey a lot to just get downhill. You would play her for the spot-up. I think her ability to play off two feet, to get to the free-throw line, to read the game in a number of ways has been really impressive. It's tough to do what she's been doing night in and night out."

Looking ahead, Clark put a positive spin on Indiana's difficult stretch by pointing out the team can quickly rebound on Sunday against the Chicago Sky before it has a few days off to recover.

The Fever have clinched a playoff berth but will want to improve their position in the WNBA standings. At 24-14, they're in fifth and only trail the second-place Golden State Valkyries by three games.

Getting into fourth would mean having home-court advantage in the best-of-three first round, and climbing to third would allow Indy to avoid the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx in the semifinals.

In general, the Fever have looked better since the WNBA All-Star break but have some areas in which they need to sharpen up over the final month.

articles.title: Dr. J Reacts to LeBron, Jaylen Brown Joining 76ers and Sounds Off on NBA Title Chances
articles.summary: While Philadelphia 76ers legend Julius Erving believes the team improved this offseason, he's not immediately crowning them NBA champions.
articles.body:
While Philadelphia 76ers legend Julius Erving believes the team improved this offseason, he's not immediately crowning them NBA champions.

Erving told TMZ Sports he gave the Sixers a "thumbs up" for the Jaylen Brown trade, adding they will be "one of the most talented teams." The Hall of Famer does, however, have some questions about a lineup that includes 41-year-old LeBron James and 21-year-old VJ Edgecombe.

"There's a big age discrepancy between the youngest, you know, which is VJ, and LeBron," he said. "So how that works, it remains to be seen."

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

Erving compared the roster to experimenting with a new dish in the kitchen you've never tried.

"You're trying to create something special. You're trying to create something," he said. "You go in the kitchen and you mix the ingredients, and then once you put fire under there, you see whether it's going to be good, great, or OK."

Erving's assessment probably represents the general consensus on Philadelphia.

On paper, a starting five of James, Brown, Edgecombe, Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey is the best in the NBA. Getting all of the pieces to fit together could be tricky, though, when four of the five are accustomed to working on the ball.

Philly is also hedging a lot of its hopes on Embiid staying healthy, which is a familiar concern. The team's ceiling changes if he's not on the floor because there's a steep drop between he and backup center Adem Bona.

The Sixers have the talent to challenge the New York Knicks for the Eastern Conference crown. Still, NBA superteams haven't fared well in recent years, so it won't be a complete shock if the experiment proves to be a bust.

articles.title: Jokic vuelve a superar a 'Wemby', pero Serbia cae sobre la bocina
articles.standfirst: Jaylen Hoard anota la canasta ganadora gala a pesar de la remontada de 19 puntos de los serbios
articles.summary: Jaylen Hoard anota la canasta ganadora gala a pesar de la remontada de 19 puntos de los serbios
articles.body: Los Francia - Serbia van camino de convertirse en la nueva gran rivalidad del baloncesto europeo y casi mundial. Y no sólo porque se enfrenten dos escuadras de enorme calidad y que siempre tratan de llegar lo más lejos posible en los torneos que compiten. Tener a dos de los cinco mejores jugadores del planeta ayuda y mucho. Decía Nikola Jokic tras el primer amistoso: "Un amigo me dijo un día que no hay amistosos, sino partidos de preparación. Siempre he entendido que cualquier partido es importante y me gusta afrontarlos así". Para el serbio no hay partidos relajados, da igual lo que haya en juego. Y lo volvió a demostrar en Orleans. Francia ganó a Serbia, 91-90, en un choque en el que de nuevo el que iba ganando se relajó y tuvo que volver a ganar el partido al final, como en el primer partido, pero al revés. Los franceses llegaron a mandar hasta por 19 cuando al descanso el marcador lucía un 54-35. Si ya en cualquier partido remontar 19 puntos es complicado, en un amistoso parece misión casi imposible. Pero no cuando está Jokic jugando. El serbio lideró a su país para que se metiera en el partido y luego los triples de Jovic y Dobric hicieron el resto. Serbia fue acortando poco a poco su desventaja con un parcial de 4-18 hasta ponerse por delante, 72-76 a falta de 6:48. Fueron entonces los franceses los que reaccionaron para volver a controlar el choque. Con Sylvain Francisco dirigiendo y Luwawu-Cabarrot anotando, Francia volvió a irse, 85-77, y ya parecía algo definitivo. Pero no, los balcánicos volvieron al partido y a cinco segundos para el final se colocaron por delante, 89-90 con una canasta de Guduric. La canasta final de Jaylen Hoard sobre la bocina en un error defensivo serbio, dio la victoria a Francia. Lo celebraron como un triunfo oficial. En Francia Francisco fue el mejor anotador con 20 puntos, mientras que Luwawu-Cabarrot hizo 19 y Wembanyama aportó 18 y cinco rebotes en 24 minutos. Jokic volvió a dar otro recital con 34 puntos, 13 rebotes y cinco asistencias jugando casi 30 minutos para 34 de valoración. Jovic anotó 13 puntos y Guduric, 11. El de Orleans ha sido el último partido de preparación de ambas selecciones. Ya en las Ventanas, Francia jugará contra Eslovenia (27 de agosto) y Suecia (30), con la tranquilidad que da su 5-1 en el grupo L, mientras que Serbia lo hará ante Islandia (28) e Italia (31), algo más apurado por el 4-2 que lucen.

His Warriors career was interrupted by Achilles and knee injuries that caused him to miss two straight seasons from 2019-21.

Still, Thompson returned to Golden State and helped the organization remain successful before signing a three-year contract with the Mavericks as a free agent in July 2024.

At the time, Dallas was coming off an NBA Finals appearance led by star Luka Dončić. The Mavericks ultimately traded Dončić to the Los Angeles Lakers during the 2024-25 season, though.

articles.summary: El partido deja claro que el trabajo de Méndez y la selección va por muy buen camino
articles.body: Una cosa ha quedado clara en Tenerife: jugando a este nivel, el demostrado ante Bélgica, España puede aspirar a cualquier cosa. 'Volvamos a soñar' es el lema de la gira de la selección y el equipo está dando los pasos para poder soñar de verdad. La selección aplastó a Bélgica, 95-67 en el tercer partido del torneo Internacional de Tenerife. Es cierto que esto es un partido de preparación y las conclusiones deben ser sacadas con perspectiva, pero ante las campeonas de Europa se vio un equipo que cada vez avanza más hacia la idea que su seleccionador quiere. Una defensa casi impenetrable que dispara luego un ataque eléctrico y muy eficiente. España llevaba cuatro derrotas seguidas ante Bélgica incluyendo dos finales de Europeos. Ganar este partido puede ser crucial si en algún momento ambos equipos cruzan sus caminos en el Mundial, que puede ocurrir. Las belgas ya saben lo que esta selección española puede dar. La puesta en escena del equipo de Méndez fue formidable. Por un lado el ataque funcionó a la perfección, y no sólo los tiros, sino también las penetraciones o los contraataques culmindos tras robo. Y todo eso con una enorme defensa que desactivó a Meeseman, su principal referente. Ya en el primer cuarto se vieron las intenciones españolas con el 25-16 al final del periodo. El despertar de Meeseman acercó a Bélgica, 33-31, pero los triples de Helena Pueyo volvieron a disparar a la selección. Al descanso, 45-42 por los siete puntos encajadas en los últimos instantes. Pero en la reanudación, las de Méndez seguían de subida y fueron disparando la ventaja. Los triples siguieron cayendo (13 anotó España de 25 intentos), demostando que si están acertadas desde el arco, es un equipo muy difícil de ganar. Una muestra del acierto español fueron los 5/8 de Pueyo, el 2/3 de Maite Cazorla y, sobre todo, el 4/4 de Elena Buenavida. La ventaja se disparó hasta los 30 puntos y una máxima de 33, 91-58, para acabar con el +28 final que quizá no da la imagen real entre ambos equipos, pero que pone de manifiesto dónde está España ahora mismo. Las últimas dos pruebas de la selección serán en Zaragoza ante Mali y China. Luego, ya pueden soñar con el Mundial. Iyana Martín acabó con 15 puntos y 8 asistencias, Pueyo también hizo 15 puntos, Cazorla aportó 14 y seis asistencias y Buenavida e Irati Etxarri firmaron 12. En Bélgica, Lisowa fue la mejor con 12 y Meeseman se quedó en 10.

Klay Thompson has officially signed with the Miami Heat:

Heat still have 2 rosters spot left after signing Klay

According to The Athletic's Sam Amick and Darnell Mayberry , the veteran signed a two-year, $11.5 million contract with the Heat after reaching a buyout with the Mavs.

After clearing waivers on Sunday, he was able to officially sign with Miami.

The deal reportedly includes a player option for the second year and also includes a 15 percent trade kicker.

The Mavericks announced Friday that they are buying out the final year of Klay Thompson's contract. The five-time All-Star was due to earn $17.5 million for the 2026-27 season

Dallas' move is a sign of how far Thompson's value has diminished around the NBA. Once one of the best two-way players in the league, he fell out of the Mavericks' starting rotation midway through last year.

In 69 appearances, he averaged 11.7 points and set career lows in overall field-goal percentage (39.3) and three-point percentage (38.3).

Jason Kidd shifted Thompson to the bench after seven games, which made for a delicate situation considering Dallas promised him a starting spot when it made its pitch during the 2024 offseason.

Kidd indicated it was only a temporary tactical change, and the 36-year-old was with the first unit again in a loss to the New York Knicks in mid-November. But he eventually assumed a reserve role again.

The Warriors saw the writing on the wall with a player who had become a franchise icon.

Head coach Steve Kerr and general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. were pragmatic rather than sentimental with Thompson's usage during the 2023-24 season and then regarding how they approached his subsequent free agency.

Breaking up the "Splash Brothers" wasn't a move anybody in the Bay Area wanted to make, but the Warriors understood Thompson was on a downward trajectory. Missing two full seasons because of a torn ACL and a torn Achilles accelerated the inevitable decline that was coming as he got older.

A change of scenery and a desire to prove Golden State wrong didn't spark a renaissance in his first year with Dallas. He averaged 14 points per game, his lowest output since his rookie season, and his field-goal percentage (41.2) was a personal worst at the time.

The Mavs knew they weren't getting Thompson at his peak when they signed him. They presumably envisioned him occupying a role similar to Ray Allen during his two-year run with the Miami Heat and toward the end of his Boston Celtics tenure. Allen remained a capable three-point specialist as his career wound down, shooting 37.5 percent from beyond the arc in his final season.

Thompson's long-range prowess has even started to desert him, though, which makes the other flaws in his game tougher to ignore. He's not as dogged a defender and he can't score off the dribble like he once did.

The days of Thompson being a big difference-maker on a contender may be over, but he's a low-risk addition for a Heat team that saw Giannis Antetokounmpo enter the fold this summer.

articles.title: Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham's Final Box Score Stats, Highlights as Fever Beat Sky
articles.summary: The Indiana Fever's short losing streak is over.
articles.body:
The Indiana Fever's short losing streak is over.

Indiana ended its two-game losing streak and improved to 25-14 on the season with a 113-90 victory over the Chicago Sky on Sunday. Caitlin Clark and the Fever entered the contest as 3.5-point favorites on FanDuel Sportsbook and finished the season sweep of Chicago even though Aliyah Boston was sidelined with a lower leg injury.

Clark and Kelsey Mitchell continued their season-long brilliance with 14 combined three-pointers, while Sophie Cunningham added three points off the bench. Natasha Cloud led the way for Chicago in a losing effort, but there was only so much she could do to counter Clark making more history:

Indiana entered the game on a poorly timed mini-slide that knocked it into fifth place in the standings that have just a handful of games separating the second seed from the eighth seed. The standings flip with seemingly every result, so Sunday was an important opportunity to bounce back against an opponent they have controlled play against this season.

Yet Chicago was ready to put up a fight in the early going.

The home team used a balanced attack to seize a 51-50 halftime advantage with eight different players scoring at least four points before intermission. The Sky's bench provided a much-needed boost, which helped counter Clark dominating play on an individual level with her combination of outside shooting and facilitating when defenders collapsed.

Makayla Timpson also got off to a quick start for Indiana, which helped make up for the loss of Boston. Clark even found her on a behind-the-back pass, although the visitors still found themselves behind early due to their defensive issues without their frontcourt star.

Still, offensive dominance is often enough to overcome defensive woes on the other side, as Clark and Mitchell reminded the Sky in the third quarter.

The duo of backcourt stars took over with an array of deep threes, floaters and drives into the lane, and Chicago had no answer. Frankly, there may be no team in the entire league that will have a counter for the guards when they are both playing at their best, although the Sky were still well within striking distance heading to the fourth thanks in part to an offensive flurry from Cloud.

But there would be no fourth-quarter rally for Chicago.

The Clark and Mitchell show led the way, but the Fever finally dialed up the defensive intensity when the game was on the line as well. The Sky failed to generate any offensive momentum until it was too late, and it would have required quite the offensive performance to overcome the two Indiana guards.

With Sunday's win secured, the Fever will now look to start a winning streak and climb the standings as they host the Connecticut Sun on Friday.

The Mystics lost 28 games and finished seven back of the eighth-place Golden State Valkyries in 2025. The general vibes around the organization were not those of a team that was well outside of the postseason hunt, though.

That's because Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen both made the All-Star team as rookies, and the 2026 WNBA draft promised to bring more reinforcements for a young core.

Citron is averaging more points (16.9) and assists (4.1) than she did last year, and Iriafen has seen a bump to her scoring (15.1) and rebounds (9.3). Both are taking steps forward in their development.

Shakira Austin, meanwhile, has expanded her offensive repertoire. Seventeed made three-pointers may not seem like a lot, but they are for a player who knocked down three total threes through her first four seasons.

Depth behind the starting rotation has come from 2026 first-rounders Lauren Betts and Cotie McMahon. Georgia Amoore, who missed her entire rookie campaign through injury, is second on the team in assists (3.5).

Ironically, the 25-year-old Amoore is one of the oldest players.

Washington is bucking almost every historic precedent. Teams with rosters this young have by and large been very, very bad.

Even when accounting for the fact the WNBA has diluted the talent pool a bit through expansion, putting together a winning record when only three players on the roster have more than one year of service time is incredible.

For right now, the Mystics are playing with house money because they're ahead of schedule in their rebuild. Winning a series would be nice, but simply having Citron, Iriafen, Betts and McMahon taste playoff basketball is important in its own right.

The postseason could also be instructive to the coaching staff and front office toward how to continue building around Citron and Iriafen.

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from WNBA game after being confronted by Sky’s Natasha Cloud
articles.summary: The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates about whether transgender women should be allowed to play in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.
articles.body: CHICAGO — Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter. Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.” The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction. Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, also 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two. “There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss. Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team. “I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.” Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby. He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena. “I didn’t see it. We were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said. “So I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.” Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media. The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game. Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players. “If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said, “and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too.”

articles.title: El nuevo Real Madrid se estrenará en la SuperCup de la Euroliga
articles.standfirst: La competición se disputará en Abu Dabi los días 18 y 19 de septiembre
articles.summary: La competición se disputará en Abu Dabi los días 18 y 19 de septiembre
articles.body: La Euroliga anunció este lunes el nacimiento de una nueva competición. Ya se habló de ello en julio, aunque no hubo anuncio oficial. Pero la nueva SuperCup ya ha recibido la luz verde y por lo tanto habrá un nuevo título que sumar a la lista de los objetivos de esta temporada. La SuperCup que se celebrará en Abu Dabi los próximos 18 y 19 de septiembre reúne un cartel de lujo: Olympiacos, Real Madrid, Fenerbahce y Dubai Basketball. Los griegos acuden por su condición de actuales campeones de la Euroliga, el Madrid por ser finalista, los turcos por ser el anterior campeón y el Dubai como equipo anfitrión. Es cierto que, como ocurre con otras 'supercopas' se trata de un torneo entre la pretemporada y el inicio oficial de la competición, pero no deja de ser un título y sobre todo con un cartel tan atractivo como el que ofrece en este caso la SuperCup. El Madrid, muy renovado, podrá poner a prueba su proyecto a las primeras de cambio contra equipos que, en mayo, estén peleando por entrar en la Final Four que, en principio, también se celebrará en Abu Dabi. El equipo de Pedro Martínez cuenta con numerosas novedades en su plantilla: el propio entrenador, Jaime Pradilla, Timothe Luwawu-Cabarrot, Mikael Jantunen, Max Shulga, Olivier Sarr y Eli Ndiaye a falta de que Damian Jones sea presentado y quizá a la llegada de un dos, aunque este podría llegar en los descartes de la NBA. El Madrid ya habrá jugado partidos de preparación ya que participará en el torneo Costa del Sol de Málaga junto a La Laguna Tenerife y Unicaja, pero no jugará la Supercopa Endesa en Badalona, que, por cierto, coincide en fechas con la europea (19 y 20). Disputar dos partidos ante equipos punteros de la Euroliga es una excelente puesta a punto para los de Martínez. Además, se da la circunstancia de que los blancos debutarán en la Euroliga precisamente en Dubái el próximo 24 de septiembre, cinco días después de jugar la SuperCup, por lo que podrán quedarse en Dubai para disputar el partido ya oficial de Liga regular. En el torneo de la Euroliga se podrán ver también algunas novedades en equipos muy favoritos como el Olympiacos: Jean Montero o Codi Miller-McIntyre, Fenerbahce: Sertac Sanli, Shavon Shields, Trent Forrest, Braxton Key, Shane Larkin o Will Clyburn, o el Dubai con el estreno de Xavi Pascual y las llegadas de Tornike Shengelia, Mamadi Diakite, Jaron Blossomgame o Elie Okobo. El formato de la SuperCup será igual que el de una Final Four. El viernes 18 se disputarán las semifinales con el Olympiacos - Fenerbahce a las 16.00 hora peninsular (18.00 hora local), y el Real Madrid - Dubai Basketball a las 19.00 en España (21.00 en Abu Dabi). El sábado habrá un tercer y cuarto puesto (16.00 en España) y la final tres horas después (19.00). "La SuperCup refleja nuestra ambición de seguir innovando y ampliando el alcance del baloncesto de clubes europeo", valoró el CEO de la Euroliga Chus Bueno. "Lanzar esta nueva competición en Abu Dabi nos permite conectar con nuevas audiencias y, al mismo tiempo, ofrecer a aficionados, clubes y socios un evento de primer nivel que exhibe lo mejor de nuestro deporte. Esperamos consolidar la SuperCup como una cita destacada en el calendario internacional de baloncesto".

articles.title: Enes Kanter provoca su expulsión en un partido de la WNBA
articles.standfirst: El turco se enzarzó en una discusión con Natasha Cloud y luego publicó varios mensajes
articles.summary: El turco se enzarzó en una discusión con Natasha Cloud y luego publicó varios mensajes
articles.body: La polémica que estalló con el anuncio de Enes Kanter de presentarse al Draft de la WNBA de 2027 porque "me siento mujer", alimentada por otro ex NBA como Royce White, no sólo está muy lejos de acabar, sino que es alimentada a lo bestia día a día. El último capítulo tuvo lugar en un Chicago Sky ante Indiana Fever y lo protagonizó el propio ex jugador turco, con un mensaje en su camiseta, una publicación en el descanso y un final abrupto que supuso su expulsión del Wintrust Arena de Chicago. Kanter se presentó en el partido con una camiseta en la que se podía leer: "Mujer. Sustantivo. Ser humano adulto femenino". El turco sigue manteniendo que en las normas de la WNBA se indica que sólo las mujeres pueden jugar en su competición. Pero según el polémico ex jugador, no hay una definición concreta del término mujer. Y mantiene que si él se siente mujer, puede jugar en la Liga. Otra de las provocaciones de Kanter llegó en el descanso. Publicó en redes un mensaje en el que ponía: "Es medio tiempo y mecesito usar el lavabo. Las reglas son las reglas", acompañado de una foto en la que se le veía en el lavabo de las mujeres. Finalmente llegó su expulsión. Natasha Cloud, jugadora de las Sky, le fue a buscar a la pie de pista, donde estaba Kanter, y se enzarzó con él en una discusión que el turco, claro, no sólo no rehuyó, sino que elevó a lo máximo. Finalmente Kanter, se ve en la imagen, fue invitado a abandonar el pabellón y lo hizo pidiendo más ruido al público y mostrando ostensiblemente el mensaje que llevaba en su camiseta. Poco después Kanter publicó un nuevo mensaje en las redes: ¡Acabo de ser expulsado de un partido de la WNBA por apoyar a las MUJERES! Que eso cale hondo, ¡AMÉRICA!. Antes había publicado otro: "Siempre son mujeres criticando a otras mujeres".  Es un capítulo más de una polémica que está a años luz de resolverse. Al menos de momento. Y lo que está ocurriendo con Kanter y la WNBA en realidad es un resumen de una sociedad dividida entre los partidarios de que los deportistas trans puedan participar en competiciones de mujeres y los que no. Y el debate seguirá.

articles.title: 1 Realistic Blockbuster Trade That Should Happen Before NBA Season
articles.summary: At this point of the 2026 NBA offseason, there are mostly just a few T's to cross and a couple of I's to dot.
articles.body:
At this point of the 2026 NBA offseason, there are mostly just a few T's to cross and a couple of I's to dot.

Except for, you know, that 22-year-old All-NBA performer who remains without a deal.

That player is Jalen Duren, whose restricted free agency was unfortunately preceded by a big playoff flop—and a huge breakout season right before it.

Clearly, there have been complications in squaring both developments, to the point that negotiations between Duren and the Detroit Pistons have reportedly taken an "awfully nasty" turn, per ESPN's Tim MacMahon .

The gap between Duren's assessment of his value, fueled by that breakout, and Detroit's, shaped by his postseason struggles, may be too wide to bridge.

So, if the business of basketball has caused irreparable damage to this relationship, then a bold sign-and-trade might be the right business move to make.

Detroit Pistons receive: Ryan Rollins, Myles Turner and 2031 first-round pick (top-five protected)

Milwaukee Bucks receive: Jalen Duren (sign-and-trade)

They know he deftly handled a starring role in their most successful regular season in 20 years. They know he is a highly impactful presence on both ends and shares a close bond with franchise centerpiece Cade Cunningham.

And they know—or can at least reasonably project—that, at 22 years old, Duren's best seasons are still in front of him.

They also happen to know they aren't comfortable giving him the kind of contract he wants . Or maybe anything close to it. They also know their offense will face spacing concerns as long as Duren (0-for-6 from three in his career) shares a frontcourt with fellow building block Ausar Thompson (38-of-186).

They may have serious concerns about the long-term viability of this combo. They know they'd be locked into it if they met Duren's contract demands (or came close to them) and ironed out an extension with Thompson. And they know if they don't give Duren the offer he wants, they could lose control of this situation should he wind up signing the qualifying offer and thus paving a path to 2027 unrestricted free agency.

This deal offers a way out. Moreover, it just might help build a more cohesive lineup, even with Detroit trading away the most talented player in the exchange.

Myles Turner's blend of paint protection and floor spacing could create a more optimized frontcourt fit with Thompson. Ryan Rollins, meanwhile, spent his 2025-26 breakout looking every bit like the secondary scorer and shot-creator that Cunningham so badly needs alongside him. Only 13 players averaged 17 points, five assists and 2.5 three-pointers this past season; Rollins was one of them—and the second-youngest of the group.

Even if Turner is probably overpaid ( three years, $83.6 million left on his deal), and Rollins is responsible for only one notable season through four NBA campaigns, that's still a solid haul for someone the Pistons don't want to (over)pay. Especially when there's a lightly protected future first tacked on to help lessen the blow for fans who will struggle to figure out why their franchise, fresh off a 60-win effort, just cut ties with a 22-year-old All-Star.

As soon as Milwaukee split from Giannis Antetokounmpo this offseason, it got busy forming its next foundation. And honestly, it's possible this club's competitive window opens quicker than people think.

Hometown star Tyler Herro is a 26-year-old with a recent All-Star selection on his resume. Jaime Jaquez Jr. is a 25-year-old who was just runner-up for an end-of-season award . Even incoming lottery pick Brayden Burries is a soon-to-be 21-year-old whose scouting report featured NBA readiness among his greatest strengths.

If nothing else, this is a young core that could grow intriguing sooner than later—especially if the front office turbo-charged it with a talent like Duren.

While the Bucks would have to ink a sizable pact with the bouncy big man, the trade cost would look quite favorable for a 22-year-old star.

Turner, who will be 31 in March, underwhelmed during the first season of a big four-year contract. Rollins has proved little to this point beyond an ability to post big numbers on a 50-loss team.

Even that draft pick should not sting too badly, since the Bucks would still have Miami's 2031 first-rounder to dangle if they felt less bullish about their own long-term outlook.

That's not a nothing package, obviously, but it also isn't what you'd expect to see for a player as young and accomplished as Duren. Given what he and his team just achieved last season, he'd be a no-brainer keeper under almost any other circumstance. This contract stalemate, however, may have created an opportunity for the right buyer.

Why couldn't that be the Bucks? They aren't a free agent destination, so they'd only normally have access to a player like this by acing a draft pick. Duren fits Milwaukee's long-term timeline.

Plus, letting go of Rollins would give more clarity to a guard group that would still feature Herro, Burries, 2025 first-round pick Kasparas Jakučionis and 26-year-old Kevin Porter Jr., who just averaged 17.4 points and 7.4 assists.

Add Duren to this group, and the foundation would feel surprisingly solid for a franchise that just traded away its longtime face. Ace a couple of developmental projects (like Jakučionis, Nate Ament, Kel'el Ware and Ousmane Dieng), and the Bucks might be ready to rise right when several Eastern Conference elites start aging out of the top tier.

Jayson Tatum's dad blunt about Celtics roster

articles.title: 30 Overreactions to the 2026 NBA Offseason
articles.summary: Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.
articles.body:
Every NBA offseason has a different theme to it.

This year's was a fun one: There was never a dull moment.

Just when you thought you might have all the splashes accounted for, something else would make a splash and send the basketball world into another reshuffling.

With action like this, imaginations are running wild about what all of this activity (or, in certain cases, inactivity) might mean for the short- and long-term future.

We can only guesstimate how things will go, which leads to a lot of overreactions. Like, say, one for all 30 teams.

Overreaction: The NBA has a new best defense.

The Hawks had last season's 10th-best defense ( fifth-best after Trae Young played his final game in Atlanta). This summer, they added 2024-25 All-Defensive first-teamer Lu Dort and fellow former shape-shifting member of the Oklahoma City Thunder Aaron Wiggins.

Couple them with what was already a wealth of defensive talent, and you're now looking at the league's stingiest defense, right?

Maybe , but let's see it in action before making such a definitive declaration. The Hawks should be all kinds of disruptive on defense. Sure, the Thunder still have a pretty terrific collection of stoppers, the San Antonio Spurs have that 7-foot-something alien everyone keeps talking about, and the Detroit Pistons employ a host of long-limbed, physical defenders.

The Hawks look poised to rank among the league's best defenses, but crowning them No. 1 already is an unnecessary rush to judgment.

The Celtics shattered expectations with a 56-win effort last season, and then promptly traded away the MVP candidate spawned during the campaign (Jaylen Brown, who landed sixth in MVP voting and second team All-NBA) for pennies on the dollar. Jayson Tatum is suddenly without a co-star, and that probably means Boston is out of the title race—for now.

The Celtics lack the high-end star power to contend for the crown right now, but they might only be an upgrade or two to rejoining the heavyweight contender ranks.

And since they have some wiggle room—a handful of first-round picks to throw around, some monster contracts coming off the books over the next few summers—they just might make those additions before the 28-year-old Tatum ages out of his prime.

Overreaction: They'll have the NBA's best backcourt in five years or less.

Those who kept an eye on Brooklyn's summer league squads surely had a chance to overindulge on optimism surrounding this year's No. 6 pick Mikel Brown Jr. and last year's No. 8 pick Egor Dëmin.

Between the former's flashy play style and the latter's ability to utilize his added muscle, they raised expectations by the minute and even gained a shared nickname along the way.

Excitement is fine (and fully warranted), but it still needs to stay within reason. This guard group has an undeniable chance to be awesome, but it remains only a possibility. Dëmin averaged 10.3 points on 39.9 percent shooting as a rookie, and Brown shot 41 percent during his lone season of college ball.

Their individual paths to stardom are steep.

Overreaction: They will regret dismantling their core.

The Hornets had a wholly ridiculous January to April stretch in which they went 33-16 with the league's best net rating ( plus-10.5 ). But they just snatched the wind from their own sails by jettisoning two key contributors (LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges) in offseason trades.

And guess what? It was the right call. Ball, a walking injury risk with less than stellar play-style reviews , brought back Naz Reid, an unprotected first-round pick, three first-round swaps and three second-round picks.

Bridges, a volume scorer with a lot of hollow stats, somehow delivered an unprotected future first. The value was impossible to pass up, and they can now grow a more accommodating and sustainable core around cornerstones Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller.

Overreaction: They blew their cap space on nothing.

This was supposed to be a transformational summer for the Bulls, and in certain ways, it was. Their front office got an overdue overhaul, and the draft lottery delivered a pair of possible building blocks (No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson and No. 15 pick Dailyn Swain). But the gobs of cap space they possessed wound up delivering only Nic Claxton, Norman Powell and Zach Collins (and hopes of a late Bennedict Mathurin addition). Yikes, right?

Well, sort of, but they had to find someone to man the middle and landed a perfectly suitable solution with the 27-year-old Claxton. And they needed someone to help pick up the scoring slack, and Powell, a 21-plus-point scorer the past two seasons, should be up to that challenge. Neither may stick around Chicago long, but that's probably the point—lean on the vets now as their prospects find their footing and then flip those players for more long-term assets when the youth is ready to take over.

Overreaction: They finally cracked the code at small forward.

Ever since Cleveland brought Donovan Mitchell to town, this organization has chased one possible solution at small forward after the next. Could that carousel finally stop spinning? That's surely the hope after this front office burned its remaining draft assets to be crowned surprise winners of the Peyton Watson sweepstakes.

This had to be encouraging, if only to see Cleveland do something in response to the many splashes made by fellow East elites. That said, it's not like Watson's arrival guarantees the Cavs finally have their missing piece at the 3. He is a stingy, disruptive defender, but his offense is very much a work in progress.

If he can't crank up the three-point volume while sustaining his newfound efficiency, it could be hard for this offense to breathe when he's slotting alongside Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Overreaction: This roster makes no sense.

The Mavericks' roster reads like it's stuck between two eras—probably because it is.

Kyrie Irving leads a veteran core that was initially brought together to give Luka Dončić a championship chance. Meanwhile, a young nucleus is starting to take shape around 2025 top pick Cooper Flagg. This group is also light on ball-handlers and heavier than it needs to be with forwards.

And yet, this might somehow be the right spot for the Mavericks at the moment. They're still figuring things out with Flagg, like how he'll fare alongside an established star like Irving (who missed all of last season while rehabbing a torn ACL).

They're also in no rush to move veterans ( other than perhaps Klay Thompson), since they could try to compete with them first, knowing they'll always maintain trade value.

Overreaction: They're giving Nikola Jokić reasons to consider leaving.

Setting aside any sentimental attachments or the desire to complete a career with one franchise, what is the great argument for Jokić recommitting to Denver ? The Nuggets are still a really good team, but is greatness a legitimate possibility? They've won two total playoff series in the three seasons since their 2023 title run, and their already compromised defense now must find a way to proceed without Peyton Watson.

All of this feels ominous, yet none of it really matters unless Jokić decides it does. And so far, nothing has changed the notion that he plans to continue his career in Denver. ( Well, nothing other than the dreams of hopeful poachers .) The Nuggets should be careful about taking his presence for granted, but it hardly sounds like he is scanning for the exits.

Overreaction: Cade Cunningham's co-star isn't coming.

The rumor mill connected the Pistons to some fascinating scenarios this summer, but nothing major materialized. Labeling their offseason dud is a bit harsh—John Collins can pile up points, and Isaiah Joe's shooting scratches a big itch—but it's certainly disappointing when weighed against some of those initial expectations, especially when nothing has been figured out with Jalen Duren yet.

This all leaves Cunningham without the co-star he seemingly needs to make a real championship push. Detroit will have more chances, though. If the Pistons can't develop that player (maybe Duren or Ausar Thompson), they'll still have the assets needed to go pursue a needle-mover in a trade.

Overreaction: They failed Stephen Curry.

As shepherds of Curry's once-in-a-lifetime career, the Warriors have some responsibility for ensuring he has a chance to play for something of significance. So, when they're effectively running back a 45-loss roster for what will be his age-38 season, it sure feels like a franchise-wide failure.

Maybe history will remember it as such, but Golden State still has a chance to field a more formidable supporting cast around him. It'll just take some time to make that happen. The Warriors have draft capital to throw around and navigable paths toward big-time financial flexibility, plus a potential difference-maker on the mend in Jimmy Butler, so things aren't nearly as dire as they may initially appear.

After following consecutive 52-win campaigns with first-round exits, the Rockets appeared open for anything this summer. They gave potential trade partners the impression that Amen Thompson was their "only near untouchable," per Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko , suggesting their roster might look dramatically different for the 2026-27 season.

When considering the potential activity, this feels a lot closer to status quo. This is not, however, a stationary squad. Fred VanVleet is back, Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović have joined the party and the young core has had another offseason of development. Splash-less summer or not, it's still a collective stock up for Space City.

Overreaction: A sleepy summer has them set up for disappointment.

Tyrese Haliburton has wondered aloud why the league isn't treating his return from a torn Achilles as a bigger deal. Clearly, expectations in the Circle City are enormous with the franchise floor general back and Ivica Zubac manning the middle.

You wonder whether expectations will be too high, though, given all that has changed in the East since Indiana booked that surprise trip to the 2025 NBA Finals.

When players like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James and (presumably) Kawhi Leonard are moving around, that activity tends to overshadow the return of a small-market's star. But Haliburton might be onto something.

This offense hums when he's at the helm, and Zubac can be a stabilizer at center. The Pacers didn't need a busy summer to drum up excitement (at least internally) around their chances for the upcoming campaign.

Overreaction: Keaton Wagler was exposed in Summer League.

With the Clippers in the process of closing out the Kawhi Leonard chapter, Wagler, their No. 5 pick, is prominently positioned for whatever comes next. So, he had plenty of eyeballs on him at summer league, and he didn't exactly thrive under the spotlight. He was an inefficient scorer and an ineffective contributor in virtually every other category.

It was disappointing to see. It was also potentially meaningless. Las Vegas has a history of fooling the hoops world with mirages . And Wagler, who impacts the game more with feel than freakish physical tools, never figured to thrive in that environment. You'd still prefer to see him star at summer league, but overreacting to the fact he didn't is pointless.

Overreaction: They just pumped all of their assets into a Play-In roster.

The Lakers prioritized a new contract for Austin Reaves and finding an impact center this offseason. They managed to check both boxes, but they paid an exorbitant cost to do it: $184.8 million for Reaves, and then two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps for the right to give Walker Kessler $129.5 million.

Luka Dončić at least seems on board with the moves , but there isn't an obvious way for L.A. to wiggle out of this should things run awry.

And maybe that's OK. Dončić plus a second scorer and shot-creator has proved an awful potent combo in the past. Dončić plus an impact center has typically delivered results, too. If L.A. works some developmental magic on the likes of Cameron Carr, Adou Thiero and Quentin Grimes, this roster could surprise sooner than later.

Overreaction: Cameron Boozer should've been the No. 1 pick.

Did anyone catch Boozer's run with the summer-league Grizzlies? You might still be cleaning up drool puddles if you did. He was any and everything he was billed to be: versatile, productive, efficient and absolutely impactful on winning.

So, should he be cemented on way-too-early re-draft boards now? Nope. The skills he showed in summer league were never questioned; any knocks were always tied to the fact he lagged behind both AJ Dybantsa and Darryn Peterson in terms of physical tools, which is clearly still the case. Boozer might already have the highest floor of the three, but teams holding the No. 1 pick are seeking more than safety.

Overreaction: Landing a whale unlocks immediate championship possibilities.

For years, the Heat waited for this very opportunity—not simply landing a superstar, but getting Giannis freakin' Antetokounmpo. And given how successful they'd managed to be in some of those superstar-less seasons, his addition has to make them an immediate factor in the championship chase, right?

Well, you never want to rule out anything involving a player this talented, but this roster has question marks all around the Antetokounmpo-Bam Adebayo combo (which has its own logistical concerns with spacing). Throw in the rising tides of a fully loaded East, and Miami isn't guaranteed a top-six seed, much less a legitimate shot at winning it all.

Overreaction: They botched the Giannis Antetokounmpo blockbuster.

By the time the Bucks got around to trading away Antetokounmpo, he was entrenched as the best player in franchise history. And through that lens, Milwaukee's return package—Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, Kasparas Jakučionis, three firsts, a swap and a second—might seem so underwhelming to make you think the Bucks really botched this.

They didn't. Or they didn't botch it this offseason, at least. Teams weren't beating that offer (especially if Milwaukee thinks the homegrown Herro is a keeper) for a 31-year-old with shooting limitations, contract uncertainty and some recent injury trouble. The Bucks just needed to rip this Band-Aid off sooner. Everyone outside of Milwaukee could see this coming and delaying the inevitable denied this club what could have been a truly ridiculous collection of incoming assets.

Overreaction: Anthony Edwards has a championship chance now.

The Wolves needed more consistent offensive support for Edwards and just found it in LaMelo Ball, a nightly 20-point, 10-assist threat with deep shooting range, two-steps-ahead passing vision and gobs of creativity. This was someone whom Minnesota's decision-makers "had long believed was the ideal backcourt running mate for Anthony Edwards," per The Athletic's Jon Krawczynski .

The Wolves' working theory is a fun one. It's also risky as heck. Minnesota effectively drained its asset pool and changed identities for an offense-leaning (or offense-only) player who owns a career 41.8 field-goal percentage and has reached the playoffs exactly zero times. Oh, and he has played fewer than 52 games in four of his six seasons. It would be objectively awesome if this works, but the list of reasons to believe it won't is not a short one.

Overreaction: They missed their window to reset.

Sellers were in top demand this offseason as there weren't enough impact players to satiate the many buyers. Shouldn't the Pelicans have used that to their advantage? Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones should've had rich markets, and Zion Williamson might've even been movable after making 60-plus appearances for the second time in the last three seasons.

For whatever reason, though, the stars never aligned on a swap. Maybe that was a major misfire by New Orleans, but executive vice president of basketball operations Joe Dumars told NOLA.com's Rod Walker the inactivity was "not from a lack of effort or us deciding we didn't want to do anything." The Pelicans seemingly just didn't back down from the prices they set, and there's a chance their patience will be rewarded the next time trade season gets rolling.

Overreaction: Their roster won't be the same without Mitchell Robinson.

It could be ages before the Knicks wind up with a player as big and bouncy as Robinson. The 7-foot rim-runner may not have been the most durable player around, but he always made his presence felt in small doses. Despite often operating opposite New York's stacked starting lineup, Robinson managed to post a plus-2.6 net differential .

New York will miss Robinson's paint presence and anti-gravity ups, but not in a this-club-can't-repeat kind of way. The Knicks gave him fewer than 20 minutes in the regular season and trimmed that to less than 14 in the playoffs, so they're only filling a niche role. And Andre Drummond should be a serviceable replacement, especially on a minimum contract.

Overreaction: Dynasties are impossible in the NBA's economic environment.

The Thunder won 132 regular-season games and six playoff series over the past two seasons. They traded away three rotation regulars over the offseason, and not to accommodate newcomers but rather to make the budget more manageable. Such is life under this collective bargaining agreement.

Or is it? Because these maneuvers weren't apron-related. As The Athletic's Fred Katz relayed, "In the league's third-smallest market, owner Clay Bennett is sticking to a budget."

Other organizations won't give themselves the same restrictions, meaning their budgets could certainly stretch farther than this, especially if doing so meant keeping a potential dynasty together.

Overreaction: They're denying the reality of their wing tandem.

The Magic just played their fourth season with both Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner on the wing. They even propped up that pairing with a bold (and budget-busting) trade for Desmond Bane. Yet, they're still awaiting the first playoff series win of the Banchero-Wagner era. Perhaps because this twosome just doesn't work.

But the Magic are right for thinking it's too soon to make that call. A coaching change could help better align the puzzle pieces. And there are still ways to tweak this core without demolishing the foundation. Teams rarely improve by trading their best players away.

Overreaction: This offense has too many mouths to feed.

Every time a superteam is spawned, the same concern rises shortly thereafter: There's only one basketball to go around . As if that reality doesn't exist for every other team in the Association.

Will it be simple to satisfy all four of LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Tyrese Maxey and Joel Embiid? Nope—but that's a problem that just about every other franchise would love to try tackling.

"Talking to (head coach Nick Nurse), he's excited. It's just like a kid in a candy store," Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey told reporters . "He's like, 'How are we going to put this thing together and see if it works?'"

When that one basketball goes around, it will often find its way to either a former MVP or a current All-NBA honoree. If Philly can strike the right balance, this offense should be silly.

Overreaction: Devin Booker still has no help.

The Suns stripped themselves of a Booker co-star when they traded Kevin Durant last offseason. At this rate, it doesn't feel like they're even searching for one. When they're adding talent, it's of the role-playing variety: Miles Bridges as a scoring forward, Luke Kennard as a net-shredder, Koa Peat as a forceful dot-connector.

Maybe this all means the whole outpaces the sum of the parts again. Phoenix overpaid for Bridges, but it did have a void to fill at power forward. It signed a lot of sensible contracts, which should remain movable if a direction change is needed. And things aren't even helpless on the co-star front, as big developmental leaps could still be in front of Jalen Green and Khaman Maluach, and the regression that was supposed to hit Dillon Brooks in the playoffs never came close to materializing.

The Blazers saw an offer they couldn't refuse. That's the only rationale that makes sense behind their summer swap of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for Ja Morant. And honestly, that reasoning is sound. It's sort of a no-risk, all-reward wager on a two-time All-Star who just turned 27. In a vacuum, there's a lot to love.

Basketball teams don't play in a vacuum, though, and this is one situation where the old there's only one ball thing feels legitimately worrisome. How does a roster simultaneously squeeze the most out of Morant, Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday? And how does that guard group not totally torpedo the on-ball opportunities for All-Star swingman Deni Avdija? Even in a positionless league, there are too many cooks in this kitchen.

Overreaction: Darius Acuff Jr. is doomed.

Summer league was rough for Acuff. His scoring volume reached an acceptable level, but that was it for positives. His efficiency underwhelmed, his playmaking unraveled amid a sea of turnovers and his defense lived up to its unfavorable billing.

None of that necessarily matters, though. Acuff handled a heavy responsibility list as a teenager in a chaotic environment. Things going well may have been more surprising than these struggles.

As far as there are worries with Acuff, who won't turn 20 until November, they hinge more around his chances of germinating in what has been, shall we say, less than fruitful soil in Sacramento.

Overreaction: De'Aaron Fox has got to go.

The NBA Finals put the worst kind of spotlight onto Fox. He not only struggled in major moments, he also saw the player right behind him on the depth chart, last summer's No. 2 pick Dylan Harper, succeed in such a way that everyone wondered why he wasn't getting more minutes . The worst read on the situation painted Fox as a $221.7 million obstacle in San Antonio's path.

That's not at all how the Spurs see it, though. General manager Brian Wright expressed "the ultimate faith in De'Aaron," and The Athletic's Jared Weiss relayed that "multiple team and league sources said the Spurs still see Fox as a critical piece of the team's future." This is how San Antonio needs to handle this, since it has enough floor time and touches to get the best out of its three-headed monster in the backcourt, and it needs the on-court organization Fox offers.

Overreaction: Summer League proved Allen Graves was a steal.

Graves was a curiosity in college, a reserve on a mid-major with some of the best analytics around. Toronto snatched him up with this summer's 19th pick, and he immediately showcased his versatility on the summer circuit: 16.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 2.3 steals across four contests.

It was a proof-of-concept performance for everyone who saw him as a potential Swiss Army knife.

It was also maybe indicative of nothing for his future. His lack of athleticism could be a real challenge against actual NBA defenders, and his outside shooting still has to prove sustainable with a significant increase in volume.

This isn't to say Toronto fans should abandon hope. It's just a reminder that those hopes are nothing more than that at this stage.

Overreaction: Darryn Peterson isn't a playmaker.

Peterson's improvement as a playmaker in high school played a big part in his standing as a top 2026 draft prospect. Then, he went to Kansas and totaled exactly as many turnovers as assists (38 each) in 24 games. Next, he technically fared slightly better at Sacramento—26 assists against 24 turnovers in five outings.

This could be a cause for major concern, but it's too early to really raise that alarm. For one, he could star without a ton of passing production as an all-purpose shotmaker in a multi-distributor offense. Second, he showed advanced passing reads as a prep star, and he might just need better health and superior scoring help around him to get back into that bag.

After three straight seasons with 64-plus losses, the Wizards are putting their losing ways behind them. Washington has organically grown a compelling young core and then supplemented it with established stars (Trae Young, Anthony Davis) and the No. 1 pick in a highly celebrated draft (AJ Dybantsa).

The Wizards even brought back Khris Middleton and turned their attention toward DeMar DeRozan after a failed courtship of Russell Westbrook.

Clearly, Washington thinks it is ready to turn the corner. A bit of brake-pumping feels warranted. Young is a one-way contributor, Davis can't stay on the court (and isn't a lock to stick around) and this young nucleus has won nothing at this level.

The future is bright—there's no denying that—but Washington may not be out of the woods just yet.

Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark and actor Jason Sudeikis had a quick chat following Indy's 113-90 win over the Chicago Sky on Sunday.

articles.title: No Issues for Sophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington as Fever Beat Sky in Rematch
articles.summary: CHICAGO (AP) — The rematch was no big deal.
articles.body:
CHICAGO (AP) — The rematch was no big deal.

There were no major issues for Sophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington in Indiana's 113-90 victory over Chicago on Sunday night. Cunningham scored three points for the Fever in 11 minutes, and Carrington had seven points for the Sky in 18 minutes.

It was the first matchup between the teams since Cunningham was taken down by Carrington on a fast break earlier this month. Carrington was listed as questionable with a left foot injury, but she was cleared after going through warmups.

Enes Kanter Freedom Ejected from WNBA Game

Cunningham downplayed any lingering animosity between the teams going into the game. Indiana had dropped two in a row.

"My mindset has never changed. I think it is what it is," Cunningham said. "I'm locked in on tonight. ... I think we're just out here trying to get the win."

Cunningham and Carrington both checked in for the first time with 3:04 left in the first quarter. There were no disputes of note between the two players all night long.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he didn't have any conversations with his players before the game about the charged atmosphere for their previous matchup.

"That kind of was what it was last game and anything that came out of it kind of lasted for that time," Marsh said. "But for us, again, it was on to the next one in front of us."

Cunningham was going up for a layup in the first quarter of Indiana's 90-86 win on Aug. 8 when Carrington came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in. Cunningham got up, charged Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was windup, impact and follow-through on the foul, resulting in Carrington's ejection.

Shortly after she was thrown out, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media and tagged the Fever. Carrington is Black and Cunningham is white.

Days later, Carrington posted that she never claimed the assessment of the Flagrant 2 was the result of white privilege, but she didn't elaborate any further.

"I (couldn't) care less about what she does, what she tweets, any of that," Cunningham said before Sunday's game. "I'm here to play basketball.

"There's going to be people who are going to talk about it ... but to me, it's just another basketball game."

articles.title: Rose the Glitter-Breathing Dragon Revealed as New Mascot for WNBA's Portland Fire in Video, Photos
articles.summary: The Portland Fire unveiled their new mascot during Sunday's 105-100 loss to the Washington Mystics.
articles.body:
The Portland Fire unveiled their new mascot during Sunday's 105-100 loss to the Washington Mystics.

The organization hyped up the reveal by building a fake crater outside of Moda Center:

The otherworldly being that arrived on earth was Rose, the Glitter-Breathing Dragon:

"As the Fire returned to the court in 2026, Rose represents the Fire's spirit and relationship with Portland: passionate, unapologetic, and radiant," said Kimberly Veale, the Fire's senior vice president of marketing and communications. "She's a living modern force, embodying the vibe and self-assurance of a true Portland individualist that inspires us to truly flourish. As we get to know her, it's clear that she's got a little edge, a lot of personality, and after two decades waiting for her team to return, plenty of catching up to do."

Rose was unable to bring Portland any luck Sunday, and the Fire are on the brink of being eliminated from playoff contention. The game was a fabulous occasion nonetheless.

articles.body:
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected after a ‌verbal altercation with WNBA player Natasha Cloud of the Chicago Sky during the third quarter of Chicago’s loss to the visiting Indiana Fever.

Kanter Freedom, sitting ⁠courtside, stood up and took ⁠a few steps towards the court with his arms outstretched after Cloud began pointing and yelling at him at the start of an Indiana timeout on Sunday.

A game official and security personnel got between them, and her teammates pulled Cloud away. The official ⁠gestured for Kanter Freedom to be ejected, and he was escorted from his seat by team and arena security.

Kanter Freedom, 34, wore a black T-shirt that read: “WOMAN noun. Adult human female.”

Cloud, 34, spoke with team and league security after the Sky’s 113-90 loss but did not address the media. ⁠She did post a statement on social media, per CBS Sports.

“To every trans kid/person, You are a part of MY community & tribe. You belong. You’re loved. You’re seen. You’re perfect as you are. & you will always be protected by me,” Cloud wrote.

Kanter Freedom, who had a conversation with police officers before exiting Wintrust Arena, later wrote on his X account, “I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN! Let that sink in, America.”

Sky coach Tyler ‌Marsh said at his postgame news conference that Cloud did not want to be a distraction.

“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her we all embrace her as someone who protects our team and people who need to be protected. Tash is always gonna stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”

Marsh also had a message for spectators, apparently with Kanter Freedom in mind.

“There’s so many good things about this league and so many good things about the play of these players, that if you come to a game, you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” Marsh said.

“That seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a ⁠former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that, too.”

Kanter Freedom, formerly known as Enes Kanter, played ⁠centre for 11 years in the NBA for five teams from 2011-12 to 2021-22 and averaged 11.2 points, 7.8 rebounds and 21.5 minutes in 748 regular-season games (259 starts).

He also has spoken out on social issues, including the debate about transgender athletes. The WNBA, which has never had a known transgender player, has been ensnared in the issue, only heightened ⁠when the Fever’s Sophie Cunningham came out strongly in favour of women’s sports being solely for women.

Cunningham emphasised in her remarks last month in an ESPN profile that “girls should never have to compete with biological men”.

Cunningham later ⁠said on July 22 that she does not “dislike anyone” and that there is “room to love everyone”. She continued, “I’m ⁠also there to love biological women, and I think that there are rights that need to be protected. And, like I said, I’m gonna stand true to that. I’ll never falter in my beliefs in that. But I have never once stated that I hated the trans community.”

There have been rallies outside WNBA arenas involving people who are both pro-Cunningham and ‌anti-Cunningham.

Kanter Freedom and another former NBA player, Royce White, have talked about being eligible for the 2027 WNBA Draft, and both claim to now identify as women, according to media reports.

The league does not have a public policy about transgender participation. The collective bargaining agreement, signed in March, states ‌that “only ‌players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA”.

Cloud is in her 11th season in the WNBA and first in Chicago. She entered Sunday averaging 11.4 points, 5.0 assists, 3.6 rebounds and 29.1 minutes in 36 games (23 starts).

She has also played for the Washington Mystics (2015-19, 2021-23), the Phoenix Mercury (2024) and the New York Liberty (2025).
